newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldovan president takes election lead.
newsitem.headline: Moldovan president takes election lead.

text.p: President Mircea Snegur took a commanding lead in the first round of Moldova's presidential election, but he faces a run-off against parliamentary chairman Petru Lucinschi, early results showed on Monday.
The Central Electoral Commission said that, with 93 percent of Sunday's vote counted, the centre-right Snegur had won 39 percent. Turnout was 67 percent.
But Snegur, who was backed by several nationalist groups, was well short of the 50 percent needed to win in one round.
A run-off with Lucinschi, who presents himself as a moderate centrist and who won 28 percent of the vote, will be held on December 1.
Other contenders, including Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, were far behind on Sunday. Sangheli got just nine percent of the vote, one point behind communist leader Vladimir Voronin.
Nationalist Valeriu Matei received nine percent and four other candidates were on two percent and less.
Snegur, speaking on national radio after the early results came out, described his victory as a rebuff to conservatives.
"The...votes cast for me are a resolute rebuff to all revanchist and conservative forces of the left," he said.
"We have two more weeks -- enough time to mobilise forces and win in the second round."
Lucinschi issued his own statement, saying he was confident of victory and one of his aides said Lucinschi expected the backing of defeated candidates Sangheli and Voronin.
"In this case, our victory is more than probable," Vladimir Solonari told Reuters.
Sunday's poll was the first multi-candidate presidential election in the landlocked former Soviet republic, which is sandwiched between Ukraine and Romania.

Moldovan nationalists have long sought a union with Romania, which shares a common language and culture. Snegur advocates stronger ties with Bucharest, but he has also said Moldova should remain independent.
The campaigns of Snegur and Lucinschi were contrasting.

Snegur, 56, was aggressive and populist, criss-crossing the impoverished country of 4.3 million with a simple message: "I feel for you and, if you give me four more years and more powers I'll help you."
He has vowed to amend the constitution, probably through a referendum, to turn Moldova into a presidential republic and to force the government and parliament out.
Lucinschi, 56-year-old bespectacled intellectual, has accused Snegur of acting in an unconstitutional way and leading Moldova towards confrontation.

Lucinschi, the former leader of the Communist Party in Soviet Moldova also said he was best placed to settle the conflict with separatists in Dnestr, a predominantly Slav region in the east of the wedge-shaped country which fears that they could lose out if Moldova moved closer to Romania.
Many voters also believed Lucinschi would help develop ties with Russia, Moldova's main market and energy supplier.
